chief_complaint: chronic burning pain along incision line 3 months after surgery
hpi_details: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with chronic burning pain along incision line 3 months after surgery. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks an internal surgical stitch never dissolved properly or a deep infection is lingering under the incision scar.
concerns: She is worried that the persistent burning means the lung tumor they removed is already growing back along the scar line.
expectations: She hopes to be prescribed a numbing skin patch or soothing ointment so her clothes don't hurt to wear and she can sleep on her side.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Thoracotomy Pain Syndrome (Intercostal Neuralgia) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Thoracotomy Pain Syndrome (Intercostal Neuralgia) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Post-Thoracotomy Pain: Gabapentin, topical lidocaine patches, intercostal nerve block, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Post-Thoracotomy Pain.
Relevant background/PMH: Thoracotomy 3 months ago, otherwise unremarkable
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Thoracotomy Pain Syndrome (Intercostal Neuralgia).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Wound infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or wound drainage — suggests infection instead of neuralgia.
management_principles: Plan for Post-Thoracotomy Pain: Gabapentin, topical lidocaine patches, intercostal nerve block
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Chronic nerve pain along a surgical incision from intercostal nerve injury during thoracic surgery, persisting well beyond normal wound healing.
differentials: Recurrent disease at the surgical site
red_flags: Fever or wound drainage — suggests infection instead of neuralgia

must_ask.say: How many months ago was your chest surgery?
Does the pain feel burning or electric, along the incision line?
Does the incision look normal, or is there any redness or drainage?
Does touching the area or certain movements make it worse?
How is this pain affecting your daily activities?

history.answer: Ever since my chest surgery three months ago, I have had this constant burning pain along my scar that won't go away.
I had a thoracotomy three months ago, and while the surgical soreness improved at first, this burning sensation started about a month ago and has gradually worsened.
The burning is right along the surgical cut on the right side of my chest, following the curve of my rib.
It doesn't shoot to my neck or down to my belly, but it wraps around along the rib cage toward my back.
It feels like a sharp, burning, and raw sting, almost like a bad sunburn under the skin.
On a scale of one to ten, it usually stays around a four, but when something brushes against it, it spikes to a seven.
The pain is pretty much constant throughout the day, and it has been slowly getting worse over the past few weeks.
Even the light touch of my clothes rubbing against it, taking a deep breath, or twisting my torso makes it flare up.
Resting quietly and wearing loose, soft shirts helps a little bit, but nothing takes the burning away completely.
The incision looks fully closed and dry, without any redness or swelling that I can see.
The area around the scar feels strangely numb in spots, yet at the same time it is painfully sensitive to the lightest touch.
Yes, I have been feeling quite worn out and exhausted because the discomfort is always there and disrupts my rest.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, there has been no pus, fluid leakage, or bleeding from the scar at all.
No, I don't feel short of breath, and I haven't had any cough or chest tightness.
No, I have had no palpitations, dizziness, or lightheadedness.
No, my weight has been stable, and my appetite has been normal.
I had a right thoracotomy three months ago for a benign lung nodule resection, and they told me everything went smoothly.
I tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen for a few days, but it barely made any difference.
It makes it hard to sleep because I cannot lie on my right side, and wearing ordinary clothes has become very uncomfortable.
The cut looks closed from the outside, but it burns so badly that I thought an internal stitch didn't dissolve or some deep infection got sealed inside.
I'm terrified that this relentless burning means the tumor you took out of my lung is already growing back along the scar.
I'm hoping you can prescribe a strong numbing patch or gel so my clothes don't hurt to wear and I can sleep on my side again.
Other than the chest surgery three months ago, I have been healthy with no high blood pressure or diabetes.
I had that one lung surgery three months ago, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I am not taking any regular prescription medications right now.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I might drink a small glass of wine once or twice a month at family dinners, but that is all.
I am retired and live comfortably at home with my husband.
There is no history of nerve disorders, lung conditions, or chronic pain syndromes in my family.

exam.finding: Alert, oriented, guarding her right chest, but in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, pulse 74 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Well-healed right thoracotomy scar with no erythema, swelling, warmth, or fluctuance; tenderness elicited on palpation along the intercostal space.
Allodynia to light touch and pinprick hyperalgesia along the right fifth and sixth intercostal nerve distribution along the scar.
Resonant percussion notes throughout both lung fields bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal vesicular breathing and no crackles or wheezes.
Regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Surgical incision line is completely closed and pink with no rashes, vesicles, or open lesions.
